why_them: Three of our Vienna entries stand in the Schönbrunn botanical garden: the Ginkgo of Schönbrunn (vie_004), the Pedunculate Oak near the Hietzinger Tor (vie_021) and the Yew beside it (vie_022), and none of the three has a photograph.

org: Österreichische Bundesgärten (Bundesgärten Wien, Schönbrunn and Burggarten)
why_them: They are the actual gardeners of the Schönbrunn botanical garden trees we publish (vie_004, vie_021, vie_022), so they can confirm the age estimates for the Schönbrunn ginkgo that our sources disagree on.

org: Stiftung Preußische Schlösser und Gärten Berlin-Brandenburg (SPSG)
why_them: SPSG manages both Schlosspark Charlottenburg (the Swamp Cypress ber_004 and the Karpfenteich Elm ber_018) and Pfaueninsel, where five of our Berlin trees stand including the Türeiche and the Cut-Leaf Oak, whose species identification our own file already flags as contested.

org: Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques de la Ville de Genève
why_them: The Botanical Garden Plane Trees on the central avenue by the chemin de l'Impératrice (gen_004) are theirs, and they hold the planting records that would date the avenue precisely.

Their own yearbook archive is what let us corroborate a Copenhagen tree back to 1941 during research; they are the people most likely to correct or date the Assistens Kirkegård handkerchief tree (cop_006) and the Proviantgarden mulberry (cop_001).

Two of our New York entries are theirs, the Sassafras of Green-Wood (nyc_004) and the Second Camperdown Elm at Garden Path and Pink Avenue (nyc_014), and they run their own tree tours so they know exactly which specimens we got wrong.

We publish the Kansas Hawthorn across from their Lily Pool (nyc_015) and the Caucasian Wingnut north of the Rock Garden (nyc_016); both are garden-accessioned trees whose planting dates BBG holds and we could not find online.

Their Champion Trees of DC work overlaps directly with our fourteen Washington entries, including the Montrose Park Tulip Poplar (wdc_011) and the Battery Kemble Chestnut Oak (wdc_003), where we have honest but approximate pins they could sharpen.
The Dumbarton Oaks Beech Grove by the Lovers' Lane gate (wdc_014) is inside the park they steward, and we have no photograph of it at all.
Montrose Park and Dumbarton Oaks Park, home to two of our DC trees (wdc_011, wdc_014), sit inside the Rock Creek Park unit they work across, and their volunteer stewards walk those slopes weekly.

They train the Citizen Pruners who look after New York street trees, which is exactly the audience for our twenty-tree New York walk, and their volunteers stand next to the Hangman's Elm (nyc_001) more often than we ever will.

Their National Champion Tree register is a source we lean on for the Chicago champions (the Champion Boxelder chi_004 and the Champion Red Pine chi_005), and both entries would be stronger with their current measurements.

The Bur Oak Grove of Wooded Island in Jackson Park (chi_002) and the Bur Oak on the Midway (chi_001) are on their land, and Chicago is the thinnest of our US pages at six trees, so their oak inventory would decide whether it grows.

Five of our fourteen Munich trees stand in Schlosspark Nymphenburg: the Oak of the Dörfchen (muc_007), the Copper Beech and the Leaning Lime at the Badenburg (muc_011, muc_012), the Fern-leaved Beech at the Amalienburg (muc_013) and the Weeping Beech at the Schwanenbrücke (muc_014).

They tend the three Englischer Garten trees we publish: the Beech near Forstweg (muc_004), the Twin Elms by the Chinese Tower (muc_005) and the Fern-leaved Beech on the Schwabinger Bach (muc_006), all three still without a photograph.

The Röth-Linde at Gut Nederling (muc_001), the Krüner Eiche (muc_002) and the Reichs- und Friedenseiche in the Flaucheranlagen (muc_003) are municipal trees on their books, and they hold the Baumkataster entries that would confirm our age estimates.

Most of our twenty-two Vienna trees are theirs, including the Naturdenkmal planes of the Volksgarten (vie_007) and Rathauspark (vie_006) and the Field Elm on the Burggasse median (vie_018), which is a rare surviving elm they replant around.
They run Berlin's large public green sites and would know the current condition of the Great Elm of Treptower Park (ber_005), an elm-disease survivor we publish with an approximate pin.
They campaign on veteran trees nationally and their Berlin members are the likeliest people to have photographed Dicke Marie in Tegel (ber_001), Berlin's oldest tree and one of our photo gaps.

org: Kuratorium Baum des Jahres / Dr. Silvius Wodarz Stiftung
why_them: Their species-of-the-year work maps onto our species pages, and our Berlin list carries two European White Elms (ber_005, ber_018), the tree of the year they campaigned hardest on.

Six of our ten Boston trees are theirs, among them the Peters Hill White Oak (bos_002), the original 1948 Dawn Redwood by the Hunnewell Visitor Center (bos_005) and the Larz Anderson Hinoki Cypress bonsai (bos_007); their accession records are the definitive source for all six.

org: City of Boston Parks and Recreation Department
why_them: The Shaw Memorial Elms on Boston Common (bos_001) and the Dawn Redwood in the Public Garden (bos_004) are their trees, and both are English elms and a redwood whose survival they actively manage.
They fund the tree care on Boston Common and the Public Garden, so the Shaw Memorial Elms (bos_001) and the Public Garden Dawn Redwood (bos_004) are literally what their donors pay for.

org: The Morton Arboretum (Plant Clinic / Chicago Region Trees Initiative)
why_them: They run the Chicago Region Trees Initiative and the Illinois Big Tree Register, which is the source that gave us the Champion Boxelder of Edgebrook (chi_004) and the Champion Red Pine of Indian Boundary (chi_005), the only two city-limits records we could use.

Eight of our twenty New York trees stand in Central Park, including the Black Tupelo of the Ramble (nyc_002), the Elms on the Rocks by Literary Walk (nyc_012) and the Cedar of Lebanon grove near Conservatory Water (nyc_017); their arborists hold the tree data behind every one.

Stockholm is our thinnest Nordic page at four trees, and their arborist members are exactly who can tell us whether Birger Jarl's Oak at the Kristineberg interchange (sto_001) and Lyell's Oak at Fiskartorpet (sto_002) still hold the ages we published.

org: Bymiljøetaten, Oslo kommune (Oslo Agency for Urban Environment)
why_them: Munch-eika at Montebello (osl_001), the tree Edvard Munch painted, and the birches of Birkelunden (osl_003) are municipal trees they manage, and Oslo is a four-tree page we would like to grow with their register.

org: Statens Naturhistoriske Museum, Botanisk Have (University of Copenhagen)
why_them: The Ancient Cycad of the Palm House (cop_002), a Dioon edule that has been in the Palmehuset since the nineteenth century, is theirs, and it is the single hardest date in our Copenhagen page to verify.

They are the association of every Swiss municipal parks department, which is the fastest route to both our Swiss pages at once: the 1780 planes of Platzspitz (zur_001) and the Lindenhof limes (zur_003) in Zurich, and the Official Chestnut on the Promenade de la Treille (gen_001) in Geneva.

All four Zurich trees we publish are municipal, including Alfred Escher's Giant Sequoia in Belvoirpark (zur_002) and the Mammutbaum on Hohlstrasse (zur_004), and none of the four has a photograph. Their own site publishes only a web-support address (szh.egovservicedesk@zuerich.ch), so this is the department page rather than a verified mailbox.

org: NYC Parks (Department of Parks and Recreation)
why_them: Their forestry division holds the Great Trees of New York designations behind the Queens Giant (nyc_005), the Clove Lakes Colossus (nyc_007) and the Yew of Hero Park (nyc_008). Their site sits behind a bot challenge and publishes no address in the page source, so this is the contact page rather than a verified mailbox.

A long-running German tree-identification site with a reader community that photographs individual specimens, which is exactly the gap on our Berlin page where Dicke Marie (ber_001) and the Kaisereiche (ber_008) still have none. Address is Cloudflare-obfuscated on their own imprint and decoded from the raw HTML.
They catalogue German veteran trees by name and region, and their entries on Munich's Naturdenkmal oaks overlap directly with our Krüner Eiche (muc_002) and Reichs- und Friedenseiche (muc_003).

org: Suomen luonnonsuojeluliiton Uudenmaan piiri (Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, Uusimaa district)
why_them: The Helsinki region branch campaigns on protected natural monuments, which is what the King's Oak at the Pitkäkoski rapids (hel_001) and the Meilahti Ancient Pine by the Bronze Age burial cairn (hel_006) are, and both are photo gaps on our eight-tree Helsinki page.

org: Museu de Ciencies Naturals de Barcelona (Jardi Botanic + Jardi Botanic Historic)
why_them: Four of our Barcelona trees stand in their Jardi Botanic Historic at the Sot de l'Estany (the wingnut bcn_005, green ash bcn_006, ash bcn_021, sycamore bcn_022) and two of the four have no photograph.

The research institute sitting inside the Jardi Botanic on Montjuic, next to the Sot de l'Estany hollow where our oldest Barcelona survivors (bcn_005, bcn_006) grow; the obvious people to check our species identifications.
All seven Caserta trees we publish stand in their Giardino Inglese, including the Cedar of the Palco and the Yew of the Bath of Venus, and every single one of the seven is missing a photograph.

org: Museo e Real Bosco di Capodimonte
why_them: Eight of Naples' seventeen trees are theirs, in the Giardino dei Principi and the Real Fruttiera (the camphors, the Montezuma cypress, the Cretan palm that survived the war), and all eight lack a photograph.

org: Orto Botanico di Roma (Sapienza Universita di Roma)
why_them: Two of our Rome entries are theirs: the Twin Planes of the Eleven Fountains (rom_003) and the Cork Oak of the Orangery (rom_004), and the cork oak still has no photograph.

org: RAMI - Il Registro degli Alberi Monumentali d'Italia
why_them: We cite their field records as a source on a dozen Rome trees, including the Magnolia of Via Corsini and the Holm Oak of Piazza Perin del Vaga, where their access note settled whether the tree could be visited at all.

org: Istituto Italiano di Studi Germanici (Villa Sciarra)
why_them: The institute occupies the villa in the middle of Villa Sciarra, and rom_011 is literally the Himalayan Cedar of the German Institute standing in their own grounds; the Area acquisti e servizi generali is the office that looks after the building and garden.

org: Musei in Comune Roma (Sovrintendenza Capitolina, Villa Torlonia and Villa Borghese museums)
why_them: The Cedar of Lebanon of Villa Torlonia (rom_018) stands at the entrance staircase of their own Casino Nobile, and the Hackberries of the Aranciera (rom_022) grow beside the Museo Carlo Bilotti in Villa Borghese; both are unphotographed.

org: Patronato del Real Alcazar y de la Casa Consistorial de Sevilla
why_them: Two Seville entries are inside their walls: the Ginkgo Grove of the Jardin Ingles (sev_001) and the Pecan in the Jardin del Marques de la Vega Inclan (sev_014), and the pecan has no photograph.

org: Jardi Botanic de la Universitat de Valencia
why_them: Their Kashmir Cypress (vlc_010) and Caucasian Elm (vlc_015) are two of Valencia's sixteen trees and neither has a photograph on our page.

The Cypress of the Plano de la Flor terrace (mad_005) and the Caucasian Elm of the Paseo de Mutis (mad_006) are theirs, and their Unidad de Jardin y Arbolado is the team that measures exactly the trees we describe.

Four of our Barcelona trees are inside their park: the Carob of the Viaduct (bcn_002), the Regrown Carob of the Placa de la Natura (bcn_003), the Wild Olive of the east sector (bcn_016) and the Mastic of Hort de l'Avi (bcn_033); three of them have no photograph.

They are the people who prune and assess exactly the trees we map, and the Ombu of Placa Prim in Barcelona and the Ombu of La Cartuja in Seville are the kind of structurally odd veterans their members write about.

org: Asociacion Espanola de Parques y Jardines Publicos (AEPJP)
why_them: Their membership is the municipal parks departments of Madrid, Barcelona, Seville and Valencia, which is where most of our 100-plus Spanish trees stand, from the Retiro's ahuehuete to the Parque de Maria Luisa hackberries.

They run Spain's singular-tree work and would recognise El Titan, the giant ficus of Valencia's Parterre, and Seville's El Gran Capitan, both of which we publish and one of which we still cannot illustrate.

org: Societa Botanica Italiana (Gruppo Orti Botanici e Giardini Storici)
why_them: Their botanic-garden group covers the four Italian gardens we lean on hardest: the Orto Botanico di Roma, Brera in Milan, the Orto Botanico di Napoli and Florence's Giardino dei Semplici, where six of our fifteen Florence trees stand.

org: ISA Italia - Societa Italiana di Arboricoltura
why_them: Their arborists are the people who assess the veteran planes we publish in Milan's Giardini Montanelli, including Il Sacerdote and the 34-metre plane, neither of which we have a photograph of.

Their Rome section campaigns over the historic villas where half our Rome list stands, Villa Borghese, Villa Sciarra and Villa Doria Pamphilj, including the Cedar of the Belvedere above the Lago del Giglio.
The Cedar Above Pegasus (flo_008) stands in their Giardino del Cavaliere at the top of Boboli and is one of the Florence trees we still have no photograph of.

org: Orto Botanico Giardino dei Semplici, Sistema Museale UniFi
why_them: Six of our fifteen Florence trees are inside their walls, among them the Micheli Yew planted in 1720 and the Caucasian elm they cut back to save; the Himalayan Cedar of the Semplici (flo_014) is the one we cannot illustrate. Address published on their own page as edu(AT)sma.unifi.it.

org: Orto Botanico di Padova (Centro di Ateneo, Universita di Padova)
why_them: Four of Padua's nine trees are theirs, including Goethe's palm of 1585 and the 1786 magnolia (pad_004) which has no photograph; the address is their Settore promozione, gestione dei servizi al pubblico e comunicazione.

org: Basilica Pontificia di Sant'Antonio di Padova
why_them: The Magnolia of the Saint (pad_005) grows in their Chiostro della Magnolia, and the cloister is the one place in Padua where a visitor stands inside a monastery to look at the tree.

org: Orto Botanico di Brera (Universita degli Studi di Milano)
why_them: Their ginkgo (mil_004) is one of the two oldest in Milan and their Caucasian wingnut (mil_011) has no photograph; the garden publishes only a form, no address.

Six of our twenty Amsterdam trees stand in their garden, including the cycad in the Palmenkas that is one of the oldest potted plants in the world, plus the Turkish hazel, the twisted catalpa, the shellbark hickory, the Turner's oak and the ginkgo.
Four of Leiden's six trees are theirs: the tulip tree planted in Boerhaave's time, the ginkgo, the weeping beech by the pond and the golden chain near the entrance.
The national register of monumental trees they keep overlaps directly with the thirteen Dutch cities we publish, and they are the obvious party to check whether our ages and pins hold up.
Three of Utrecht's five trees stand in their Oude Hortus: the ginkgo, the handkerchief tree and the yew.

org: Stichting tot instandhouding van de begraafplaats Groenesteeg Leiden
why_them: The Groenesteeg beech on our Leiden page stands on the cemetery this volunteer foundation restored and maintains, and they are the only people who know its planting history.
The summer linden near the Sterckshof in their park is one of our ten Antwerp trees, and the estate's own gardeners hold its measurement history.

Rotterdam's own arboretum, three kilometres from the Park plane and the Westersingel planes we publish, and the single best-placed party in the city to correct a species or an age on our Rotterdam page.
Two of Baarn's five trees stand on their Groeneveld estate: the tulip tree grove by the ijskelder and the copper beech at the south pond.
The dawn redwood and the giant sequoia in their former Utrecht University botanical garden are two of our five Baarn trees, and we have no photograph of either.
Three of Arnhem's four trees are on their estate: De Poortwachters at the Zijpendaal entrance and the Dalweg oak in Gulden Bodem.
The juttepeer in the courtyard of the Heilige Geesthofje on the Paviljoensgracht is the opening tree of our Hague page and one of the oldest pear trees in the country.
They publish their own Hague tree walks, and our five Hague trees (Koekamp oak, Clingendael linden, Postzegelboom, Kabouterboom) overlap with the trees they campaign for.
The mulberries in their own courtyard on the Molenstraat are the first entry on our Breda page.

Three of Den Bosch's four trees grow on the city wall itself: the weichselboom on the Parklaan, the Norway maple on Bastion Oranje and the trio on Bastion Vught, which is exactly the fortification they guide people around.
The cut-leaved horse chestnut in Park Middelheim and the park trees of Kasteel Den Brandt next door are two of our ten Antwerp entries.
The Flemish tree-care association whose members manage the very parks our Antwerp and Brussels pages send people to, including Rivierenhof and the Parc d'Egmont group of six.

Flanders' forest organisation, and our Brussels page publishes sixteen trees including the Bois de la Cambre pond oaks and the Hippodrome douglas fir on the edge of the Sonian Forest they campaign for.
The black mulberry of the Jardin Botanique on the Rue Royale is one of our sixteen Brussels trees and we have no photograph of it.

They manage most of the parks our sixteen Brussels trees stand in, from Parc Tournay-Solvay and the Bois de la Cambre to the Parc de Woluwe sequoia, and they keep the regional remarkable-tree inventory.
Flanders' largest nature association, with local afdelingen in Antwerp and Brussels where our twenty-six Belgian trees stand.

They work directly with Flemish municipal green services, which is exactly who would know whether the Peace Tree on Antwerp's Grote Markt and the Millennium Ginkgo of the Stadspark are described correctly on our page.
Their local afdelingen walk the exact parks we publish, and they are the natural route to a member who could photograph the trees we still have no image of.
They already run guided walks along monumental trees in Dutch cities, which is the same walk our thirteen Dutch city pages describe.
Three of our Amsterdam trees are inside their gates: the Heimanseik, the Persian ironwood and the coast redwood, and the Heimanseik is the tree we open the Amsterdam page with.
They fight tree by tree for Utrecht's canopy, and our Utrecht page publishes the Uithof linden, the three Oude Hortus trees and the Onder de Linden row on the Nieuwegracht.
Four of our five Groningen trees are theirs to watch: the star point oaks and winter oak of the Sterrebos, the duck's foot tree in the Noorderplantsoen and the Groenestein plane.
Amsterdam is our deepest Dutch city at twenty trees, including the Olifantsiep on the Zeeburgerdijk and the Lomanstraat tunnel of planes, both of which they have campaigned about.
The Leidsebosje planes and the Amstelveld wingnuts on our Amsterdam page are exactly the kind of city-centre veterans they track.
Leiden is their region, and two of our six Leiden trees stand outside the Hortus: the Beets beech on the Burcht mound and the Groenesteeg cemetery beech.
Our four Haarlem trees are all in their patch: the Lodewijk Napoleon beech in the Haarlemmerhout, the Provinciehuis plane in the Griffietuin, the Kleverlaan yew and the Kenaupark red beech.
They keep their own page on Rotterdam's monumental trees, which covers the Park plane by the Euromast and the Westersingel planes we publish. No address is printed on their site, only a form.

They manage estates on the edge of several cities we publish, including the Sint-Pietersberg side of Maastricht where our 1700 Oaks of the Cannerbos stand. Their site publishes only a form and a privacy address.
The historic grounds of the zoo beside Antwerpen-Centraal are one of our ten Antwerp entries and the oldest planted ground in the city centre. Their site publishes a form only.
They publish a Dutch and Flemish guide to bijzondere bomen with stories, photos and locations, the closest thing to a peer we have in Dutch, and the most likely site to link to a city page.
A Dutch blog that writes regularly about remarkable trees, and a natural place for a piece on the twenty Amsterdam trees we publish.
A Flemish walking blog, and our Brussels page is a walk: six of the sixteen trees stand together in the Parc d'Egmont, which is a fifteen-minute loop off the Sablon.

org: Parques de Sintra - Monte da Lua
why_them: They run both Parque da Pena and Parque de Monserrate, which hold three of our five Sintra trees: the Walking Tree of Pena, the Araucaria of Monserrate and the Pohutukawa of Monserrate, and the Monserrate pohutukawa is still without a photograph.

source_url: https://www.regaleira.pt/ (footer, Cloudflare-obfuscated mailto decoded from the page source; geral@cultursintra.pt is published beside it)
why_them: Their neighbour Quinta do Relogio gives us the Fern Cork Oak of Quinta do Relogio, and the Regaleira grounds are the obvious next Sintra cluster for us; they are the people who would know what stands inside their own walls.

org: Jardim Botanico da Ajuda (Instituto Superior de Agronomia, Universidade de Lisboa)
why_them: The Ajuda Dragon Tree is one of the twenty-one Lisbon trees we publish and one of the few with an approved photograph; the garden's own staff are the only people who can date and check it properly.
The Lisbon nucleus campaigns on the city's own trees; we publish twenty-one of them and eleven still have no photograph, including the Strangler Fig of Principe Real and the Yew of Campo Santana.
Twelve of our seventeen Porto trees have no photograph at all, including the tulip tree and magnolia at Casa Tait, and the Porto nucleus walks these gardens.
Nine of our ten Setubal trees have no photograph, among them the Melaleuca That Grows Sideways in the Jardim Engenheiro Luis da Fonseca and the six araucarias of Largo Jose Afonso.

org: Liga para a Proteccao da Natureza (LPN)
why_them: Portugal's oldest environmental association, based in Lisbon, where we publish twenty-one trees including the olive grove at the Capela de Santo Amaro that predates the chapel beside it.
The city owns the Jardins do Palacio de Cristal, where eight of our seventeen Porto trees stand, including the Himalayan Cedar and the camellias of Casa Tait.

org: Museu de Historia Natural e da Ciencia da Universidade do Porto (Jardim Botanico do Porto)
why_them: Five of our seventeen Porto trees stand inside their garden: the Bischofia trio, the Texas Madrone, the Coast Redwood and the Atlas Cedar, and the madrone and the Atlas cedar have no photograph.

org: Museus da Universidade de Lisboa (MUHNAC / Jardim Botanico Tropical)
why_them: They run the Jardim Botanico Tropical in Belem, the one great Lisbon garden our twenty-one-tree city page does not yet cover, a gap we would rather close with their help than by guessing.
Every one of our six Bucaco trees is theirs, from Wellington's Olive at the monastery door to King Regnans in the Vale de Sao Silvestre, and five of the six still have no photograph.
The plane trees of their own gardens are the first of the four trees we publish for Guimaraes and the only one there with a photograph.
The olive tree of Nossa Senhora da Oliveira stands in their cloister and is the tree Guimaraes is named around; we publish it and have no photograph of it.

Six of our Lisbon trees stand in their parish: the fig and the dragon tree of the Jardim da Estrela, the tipu of the Jardim de Sao Bento, the tipuana and date palm of the Jardim 9 de Abril and the tipuana of Praca Sao Joao Bosco.
Principe Real is theirs, and both the Cypress of Principe Real and the Strangler Fig of the Jardim Franca Borges are on our Lisbon page; the strangler fig has no photograph.

org: Junta de Freguesia de Campo de Ourique
why_them: The Jardim Teofilo Braga, the Jardim da Parada, gives us two published trees, the taxodium and the pohutukawa, both photographed and both on their doorstep.
The olive trees at the Capela de Santo Amaro, the oldest thing on our Lisbon page, stand in their parish above the Alcantara valley.

Their own parish tree route corroborated nine of our ten Setubal trees, and we still lack photographs of nine of them, including the melaleuca that grows sideways in the Jardim Engenheiro Luis da Fonseca.

org: Dias com arvores (blog, Paulo V. Araujo and Maria P. Carvalho)
why_them: They wrote a post on the monumental cedars of the Palacio de Cristal, which is our por_008, and a book called Um Porto de arvores; nobody in Portugal is closer to what our Porto page is trying to be.

org: Amigos do Jardim Botanico de Lisboa (blog Amigos do Botanico)
why_them: They run walks called Pelo Meio das Arvores through Lisbon's historic gardens, the same gardens our twenty-one trees sit in, from the Jardim da Estrela to Campo Santana.

Our species identifications for the odder Lisbon trees, the pohutukawa of the Jardim da Parada and the ombu of Largo do Limoeiro, are exactly the kind of thing their members can confirm or correct in one line.

org: GEOTA, Grupo de Estudos de Ordenamento do Territorio e Ambiente
why_them: An urban-environment association in Lisbon; our Lisbon page maps twenty-one trees with honest coordinates, including street trees like the nettle tree of Avenida de Berlim that no walking guide covers.
Their landscape and ornamental section is the closest thing Portugal has to an arboriculture body, and our Porto page names species down to Arbutus xalapensis at the botanical garden.
They plant and campaign for trees across Portugal; we publish sixty-three Portuguese trees with locations and stories, and would rather they check our facts than find them wrong later.

org: ICNF, Instituto da Conservacao da Natureza e das Florestas
why_them: Their Arvoredo de Interesse Publico register is the backbone of our Portuguese pages and is credited on them; we also found errors worth telling them about, including three Setubal olives whose age column holds the year 2009.

org: Quercus, Associacao Nacional de Conservacao da Natureza (comunicacao)
why_them: The national office, worth writing to after the Lisbon, Porto and Setubal nuclei, because those three cities are where our sixty-three Portuguese trees are concentrated.

org: Fundacao de Serralves (Parque e Jardim de Serralves)
source_url: https://www.serralves.pt/institucional-serralves/contactos/ (the page labels an Email field but renders it in JavaScript; no address appears in the served HTML, so none is recorded here)
why_them: Their park is the one great Porto garden missing from our seventeen-tree Porto page, which currently leans on the Palacio de Cristal and the botanical garden; the biodiversity team there is the right door.

org: Porto Ambiente (municipal environment company, Camara Municipal do Porto)
why_them: They maintain the city's green spaces including the Jardins do Palacio de Cristal, where our plane of the Quinta da Macieirinha and metrosidero by the Biblioteca Almeida Garrett stand without photographs.

org: Camara Municipal de Lisboa (Direcao Municipal do Ambiente, Estrutura Verde, Clima e Energia)
source_url: https://informacoeseservicos.lisboa.pt/contactos (the city publishes no departmental address; lisboa.pt itself returns 403 to plain fetching and renders contacts in JavaScript)
why_them: The city runs the Estufa Fria and the structural gardens where most of our twenty-one Lisbon trees stand, including the Jardim Braamcamp Freire at Campo Santana whose yew and weeping fig we publish unphotographed.

They run the Cemiterio Municipal da Atouguia, whose Himalayan cedars are one of our four Guimaraes trees, and they own most of A Oficina, which manages the camellia gardens of the Palacio Vila Flor we also publish.
A small Portuguese nature title that writes about wild things you can go and see; our Lisbon walk runs from the olives of Santo Amaro to the ombu of Largo do Limoeiro with coordinates for each.
They publish Portuguese nature routes and species notes; our Setubal page maps ten trees along a walk their readers could do in an afternoon, and nine of the ten still need photographs.
They write about the Lisbon its own residents have not seen, which is exactly the giant rubber tree hidden behind Rua de Sao Cristovao in Mouraria and the strangler fig of the Jardim Franca Borges.

source_url: https://www.aoficina.pt/detail-paginas/informacoes-institucionais/ (no email published anywhere in the served HTML; the site renders contacts in JavaScript, same platform as serralves.pt)
why_them: The camellias of the Palacio Vila Flor gardens are one of our four Guimaraes trees and have no photograph; they run the gardens.
They look after the Fulham Palace Oak, the roughly 500-year-old holm oak on the Bishop's Avenue lawn that we publish as lon_007 with an approved photograph.

org: The Honourable Society of the Inner Temple
why_them: The Inner Temple Mulberry on Benchers' Walk is one of our two Temple mulberry entries and we have no photograph of it.
The Hungry Tree, the London plane swallowing a cast-iron bench by their south gate on Constitution Hill, is the single most-viewed tree we publish in Dublin.
Two of Cork's five trees stand in their grounds: the Witch's Yew in the Rock Close and the great western red cedar.
Two of Cambridge's five trees are theirs, the Main Walk giant redwood and the hybrid Cambridge Oak by the Terrace Garden, and we hold no photograph of either.
They are the volunteer group restoring the Kings Weston estate landscape where our Oak of Kings Weston stands, and they map the estate's veteran trees themselves.
They run reserves and walks across the Bristol and Bath area we cover, including ground around Ashton Court where our Domesday Oak stands.
They coordinate the UK Tree Warden network, the volunteers most likely to know and photograph the individual trees we list in London, Bath, York, Bristol, Oxford and Cambridge.
Their Notable Trees work overlaps directly with our UK city lists, and their members are the people who actually measure and photograph trees like the Totteridge Yew.
They keep the Irish Champion Tree register that underpins several of our Dublin entries, including the Glasnevin tree of heaven we call Ireland's largest.

Seven of Edinburgh's fifteen trees stand in the Botanics, including the John Muir Grove of giant sequoias and the 1948 dawn redwood on the Chinese Hillside, and only two of those seven have a photograph.
They manage both the Royal Oak near Pen Ponds in Richmond Park and the Sweet Chestnut of Greenwich Park, two of the ten London trees we published first.

org: The Honourable Society of the Middle Temple (Estates)
why_them: The Fountain Court Mulberries are ours to describe and theirs to prune; we have no photograph of them and their estates team is the only one who can say which of the two is the older.

org: Trinity College Dublin, Estates and Facilities
why_them: Three Dublin entries are inside their walls: the Provost's Plane, the champion oriental planes of New Square and the last elm of College Park.
The Camperdown Elm in their churchyard below the Castle rock is one of our Edinburgh fifteen and has no photograph.
They hold three of our Irish entries: Queen Victoria's Sequoia at Aras an Uachtarain, the Great Sycamore of Farmleigh and the 1870 Campbell's magnolia in Fota Arboretum.
Their parks service runs St Anne's Park, where we publish both the many-trunked holm oak and the Holm Oak Avenue.
Corkagh Park in Clondalkin is theirs, and its oak avenue is the one Dublin entry that sits outside the city council's area.

org: National Botanic Gardens of Ireland, Glasnevin (OPW)
why_them: Six of Dublin's seventeen trees are theirs, from the Glasnevin dawn redwood to the tree of heaven we call Ireland's largest, and not one of the six has a photograph. Their own botanicgardens.ie returns 403 to our fetches, so the address was read on the OPW's Heritage Ireland page for the gardens.
The Totteridge Yew in their churchyard is the oldest living thing we publish in London and the tree that opens the London page.

org: City of London Corporation, City Gardens
why_them: Three City trees are on their ground and all three lack a photograph: the Cheapside Plane, the Finsbury Circus pagoda tree and the planes in St Paul's north churchyard.
The Bobart Yew of 1645 in their Walled Garden is our only photographed Oxford tree, and their white mulberry beside it still has no picture.
Veteran trees are their whole subject and several of ours are textbook cases for them, including the hollow Darnley Sycamore in Glasgow and the Cammo Ash in Edinburgh.
Urban trees in exactly our cities are their work, and our London page now runs to 23 street and square trees, from the Amwell Street fig to the Marylebone elm.

org: National Trust, Prior Park Landscape Garden
why_them: The Yews of Prior Park near the Sham Bridge are one of Bath's five entries and we have no photograph of them.

org: London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham, Cleaner and Greener
why_them: Ravenscourt Park gives us two London entries, the Baobab Plane and the tree of heaven, and neither has a photograph.

He writes about London's street trees tree by tree, which is precisely what our London page does for the Amwell Street fig, the Dorchester plane and the Marylebone elm; his site publishes no address, only a Jetpack contact form.
All six York trees stand in their Museum Gardens, including the cut-leaved hornbeam and the pear-barked beech, and we also run a separate park page for the gardens.

org: The City of Edinburgh Council, Parks and Greenspace
why_them: Four Edinburgh entries are on council ground: the Cammo Ash, the monkey puzzles of Lauriston Castle, the Cramond rockface sycamore and the beeches of the Hermitage of Braid. Their site renders every address in JavaScript, so nothing could be verified; customer.care@edinburgh.gov.uk is published on their contact page but is a general switchboard.

org: Glasgow City Council, Parks and Open Spaces
why_them: Three of Glasgow's four trees are theirs: the Darnley Sycamore, the Suffragette Oak in Kelvingrove Park and the King's Park yews. Every page on glasgow.gov.uk returns a JavaScript shell, so no address could be read.

org: Bath and North East Somerset Council, Parks
why_them: Royal Victoria Park holds two of Bath's five trees, the Caucasian elm at the Royal Avenue entrance and the coast redwood in the Great Dell, and neither has a photograph. Their site renders contact details in JavaScript, so no address could be verified.

The Milton Mulberry in their Fellows' Garden, planted in 1608, is one of only two Cambridge trees we have a photograph of, and they are the only people who can confirm its condition. Their contact page publishes a form and phone numbers, no address.

org: University College Cork, Buildings and Estates
why_them: Two of Cork's five trees are on their campus, the Boole Library redwoods and the Monterey pine at the Western Road gates, and both lack a photograph. The estates pages return an empty 833-byte shell; ucc.ie's contact index lists departmental addresses but none for estates.

The Craigmillar Castle Yews are ours to describe and theirs to manage, and they are the only Edinburgh castle tree with an approved photograph. Every page on their site is JavaScript-rendered, so no address could be read.

org: National Trust for Scotland, Holmwood House
why_them: Holmwood's giant redwoods are one of only four Glasgow entries and have no photograph. nts.org.uk serves a 5KB JavaScript shell on every page, so no address could be verified.
